Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

criticism noun

finding fault; disapproval

also criticisms, criticise, be criticised, blame, censure, critical (finding fault), reproach, twit

classical

Cic. Fin. 1.1: in variās reprehēnsiōnēs incurreret
Cic. Or. 1: verērī reprehēnsiōnem doctōrum atque prūdentium (Lewis & Short)

reprehēnsiō, reprehēnsiōnis f.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

criticism, blame, censure

The commonest classical word for criticism, given or received: reprehēnsiōnem nōn fugere, not to escape criticism (Cic. Att. 10.3a.1); sine reprehēnsiōne, beyond criticism (Quint.). Properly a holding back (Cic. de Orat. 3.100).

Other words

  • vituperātiō, vituperātiōnis f. — blame, censure; the opposite of praise

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 14.13.4: in vituperātiōnem cadere (Lewis & Short); Quint. 3.4.12 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Blame as the opposite of laus; in rhetoric the speech of blame. Also blameworthy conduct (Cic. Verr. 2.5.101).

  • obtrectātiō, obtrectātiōnis f. — disparagement, carping

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Q. Fr. 1.1.43: obtrectātiōne et malevolentiā līberātum · Declension on Wiktionary

    Criticism that comes from envy or ill will.

  • cēnsūra, cēnsūrae f. — a critical judgement (of a work)

    noun, first declension · also used · post-classical · Gell. 12.2.2: jūdicium cēnsūramque facere (Lewis & Short); Ov. Rem. 362 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Classically the office of censor; as a judgement or criticism once in Ovid and then in post-Augustan prose (Vell., Plin., Gell.), and Lewis & Short thinks it probably not earlier than Augustus. Not for everyday fault-finding.

  • taxō, taxāre, taxāvī, taxātum — reproach, censure (someone for a fault)

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Suet. Aug. 4: Cassius Parmēnsis quādam epistulā sīc taxat Augustum (Lewis & Short); Suet. Dom. 10 (Lewis & Short) · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Post-Augustan, says Lewis & Short; Traupman uses it for “tease” (Traupman 33), which it does not mean.

Examples

  • Nōn eram nescius, Brūte, cum, quae summīs ingeniīs exquīsītāque doctrīnā philosophī Graecō sermōne tractāvissent, ea Latīnīs litterīs mandārēmus, fore ut hic noster labor in variās reprehēnsiōnēs incurreret.

    I was well aware, Brutus, that when I set down in Latin what philosophers of the highest talent and the most refined learning had treated in Greek, this work of mine would run into criticism of every kind.Cic. Fin. 1.1

See also attack, critic, critic, praise, assessment.
